problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/de60823bde9ec3763b3b3977467715f37bfcc205aea607b3c8eb09646ade53ce.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of a continuous function $y=f(x)$, is given above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points: 

$\,$ $x=-1\,$ and $\,x=1$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical lines $x=-1$ and $x=1.$

- We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=1.$

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-1,1),$ the point at $x=-1$ must be lower than the point at $x=1.$

So, we draw it as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/ff19d593a49c1a1938650730c5de60ec24be0c7071843b508ca4280197d34a03.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,-1)$ and increasing $↗$ on $(-1,1)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=-1.$

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-1,1)$ and decreasing $↘$ on $(1,\infty )$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=1.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x=0$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0$, and, since it is decreasing to the right of $x=0$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)<0.$ So, $x=0$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave up to concave down.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/395b5f71e3a01e51412195fbbbfbbb088fb27baddee0d15ad0d04e5ecec180f5.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/2eda7f5c16e7fddec208882a6b25871613028135896da6ab3b93e1751821743e.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
